topic.name: Reinforcement Learning
topic.description: Sequential decisions, returns, exploration, and evaluation of policies from logged interaction.

concepts.name: Reinforcement learning
concepts.description: Learning sequential decisions from rewards while actions influence future data.

concepts.name: Off-policy evaluation
concepts.description: Estimating a target policy's value from data generated by a different behavior policy.

concepts.name: Bellman reasoning and reward design
concepts.description: Relating immediate reward, discounted continuation value, and policy-preserving reward transformations.

misconceptions.name: Importance sampling works without support
misconceptions.description: Assumes a zero behavior probability can be corrected by weighting rather than making the target action unobserved.
misconceptions.remediation: Write the target-to-behavior likelihood ratio and inspect division by zero.

misconceptions.name: A learned dynamics model eliminates coverage needs
misconceptions.description: Treats model-based extrapolation into unsupported actions as identified fact rather than an assumption-sensitive estimate.
misconceptions.remediation: Separate statistical identification from extrapolation supplied by a model class.

misconceptions.name: Logged returns transfer directly across policies
misconceptions.description: Ignores that a different policy changes action choices, state visitation, and subsequent rewards.
misconceptions.remediation: Trace how the policy changes the trajectory distribution even in the same environment.

misconceptions.name: Any positive progress reward preserves the policy
misconceptions.description: Assumes locally helpful dense rewards cannot create cycles or alter the ranking of long-term returns.
misconceptions.remediation: Check whether the shaping reward telescopes as a discounted potential difference.

misconceptions.name: Discount may be omitted from potential shaping
misconceptions.description: Uses an undiscounted potential difference inside a discounted MDP, breaking the telescoping policy-invariance argument.
misconceptions.remediation: Expand the discounted return and verify cancellation requires gamma times the next potential.

misconceptions.name: Preserving terminal order makes shaping safe
misconceptions.description: Ignores path length, cycles, and intermediate reward accumulation when comparing policies.
misconceptions.remediation: Compare full discounted trajectory returns, not only terminal-state rankings.

misconceptions.name: Reinforcement learning is supervised learning on rewards
misconceptions.description: Treats observed rewards as labels for isolated actions while ignoring delayed consequences and policy-dependent data.
misconceptions.remediation: Write the return following an action and track how the action changes future states and observations.

misconceptions.name: Actions do not change future data
misconceptions.description: Assumes the learner receives an externally fixed dataset even when its choices affect state transitions and later experience.
misconceptions.remediation: Compare passive prediction data with trajectories generated under two different policies.

misconceptions.name: A greedy policy eventually explores on its own
misconceptions.description: Assumes elapsed time supplies evidence about actions that the current policy stops selecting.
misconceptions.remediation: Track action counts after an unlucky initial estimate under a strictly greedy selection rule.

misconceptions.name: Uniform random exploration is intrinsically optimal
misconceptions.description: Treats undirected random action choice as the best information strategy without considering uncertainty, regret, or state reachability.
misconceptions.remediation: Compare random exploration with uncertainty-aware or optimism-based exploration for the stated objective.

misconceptions.name: Discounting starts with the immediate reward
misconceptions.description: Multiplies the current reward by gamma rather than assigning exponent zero to the reward received at the current step.
misconceptions.remediation: Index each reward by its temporal offset in the return definition.

misconceptions.name: Discount has no role beyond random termination
misconceptions.description: Treats one useful interpretation of gamma as its complete meaning and ignores its direct weighting of delayed rewards.
misconceptions.remediation: Compute discounted returns for two reward timings even in a fixed finite horizon.

misconceptions.name: Delayed reward belongs entirely to the last action
misconceptions.description: Assigns a delayed outcome to the most recent choice without considering earlier actions that changed the state trajectory.
misconceptions.remediation: Trace return and credit across the state-action sequence leading to the delayed outcome.

misconceptions.name: Reward prediction establishes a new policy's value
misconceptions.description: Assumes accurate one-step reward prediction on logged actions identifies outcomes under actions and states poorly covered by the logging policy.
misconceptions.remediation: Audit action support, transition effects, and the policy mismatch before estimating counterfactual return.

misconceptions.name: Reward order does not affect discounted return
misconceptions.description: Treats discounted return as a function of the reward multiset while ignoring when each reward arrives.
misconceptions.remediation: Swap two rewards at different delays and recompute their gamma exponents.

questions.stem: Logged clinical decisions came from a behavior policy that never selected treatment A for a particular region of patient states. A target policy selects A there with positive probability. With no additional data, what is the central obstacle to unbiased off-policy evaluation?

options.text: There is no obstacle: assign zero importance weight to the unsupported target decisions and the estimate remains unbiased.
options.rationale: The required target-to-behavior ratio has a positive numerator and zero denominator; dropping those decisions removes target-policy mass.

options.text: Fit any dynamics model and evaluate A in simulation; model-based estimation removes the need for behavioral coverage.
options.rationale: A model can extrapolate, but unsupported action effects then depend on untestable modeling assumptions rather than nonparametric identification.

options.text: Average the observed behavior-policy returns because both policies operate in the same environment and therefore have the same value.
options.rationale: Different actions change state visitation and rewards, so behavior-policy returns do not directly estimate the target policy.

options.text: The positivity or support condition fails; the target value is not identified there without new coverage or defensible extrapolation assumptions.
options.rationale: Off-policy estimators need behavior support wherever the target assigns probability; otherwise the missing counterfactual outcomes are not observed.

questions.stem: A discounted MDP has discount gamma and a sparse goal reward. Which dense reward transformation has the standard policy-invariance guarantee, assuming bounded state potential Phi and otherwise unchanged dynamics?

options.text: Use r'(s,a,s') = r(s,a,s') + gamma Phi(s') - Phi(s), with terminal handling consistent with the potential definition.
options.rationale: The discounted potential differences telescope in returns, shifting state values without changing the ordering of action values within a state.

options.text: Add a positive bonus whenever distance to the goal decreases, because a locally progressive reward preserves optimality.
options.rationale: An arbitrary progress bonus can change path preferences or create exploitable cycles unless it has the required potential form.

options.text: Use r'(s,a,s') = r(s,a,s') + Phi(s') - Phi(s); the discount factor is irrelevant to telescoping in discounted trajectory returns.
options.rationale: In a discounted return, cancellation requires gamma Phi(s') for the next-state term.

options.text: Use any bounded dense reward that preserves the ranking of terminal states, despite intermediate paths and cycles.
options.rationale: Optimal policies depend on full discounted trajectory returns, not only the ordering of terminal rewards.

questions.stem: A recommender chooses daily lessons. Today's choice affects what the learner understands tomorrow, which lessons become useful, and the later rewards observed by the system. Why is this not adequately framed as ordinary supervised prediction of today's reward?

options.text: Each observed reward is a fixed label for the chosen lesson, so minimizing one-step prediction error solves the learning problem.
options.rationale: A reward is policy-dependent feedback within a trajectory, not a fixed counterfactual label for all available actions.

options.text: Future lesson data follow an external sampling process, so today's action changes immediate reward without changing later states or observations.
options.rationale: The scenario explicitly makes future understanding, useful choices, and collected data depend on the current action.

options.text: A later reward should be assigned to the most recent lesson, so earlier choices can be removed from the credit calculation.
options.rationale: Earlier actions can alter the state path that produces delayed outcomes, so temporal credit cannot be assigned by recency alone.

options.text: Actions influence future states and the data distribution, while delayed returns couple a current choice to later consequences under the continuing policy.
options.rationale: These are the sequential intervention and delayed-return features that distinguish reinforcement learning from passive labeled prediction.

questions.stem: In a two-action bandit, action A has one unlucky initial reward and then a greedy policy repeatedly chooses action B because its current estimate is higher. What is the core failure, and what kind of response addresses it?

options.text: The policy receives no new evidence about A after abandoning it; deliberate exploration or uncertainty-aware selection can trade short-term reward for information.
options.rationale: Greedy lock-in is caused by endogenous missing information, and exploration gives uncertain actions a route to be reevaluated.

options.text: The policy will sample A as time passes, because a greedy rule accumulates exploration evidence even for actions it does not choose.
options.rationale: Elapsed time provides no reward observations for an action whose selection count remains fixed.

options.text: Uniform random action choice is the optimal remedy, because directed exploration does not improve the information-regret tradeoff over equal sampling.
options.rationale: Random exploration is a baseline, while uncertainty-aware methods can direct samples toward actions where information has greater value.

options.text: Accurate reward prediction on logged B actions establishes A's value, so additional action support is unnecessary before changing the policy.
options.rationale: Predictions on observed B outcomes do not identify counterfactual rewards for an action with inadequate support.

questions.stem: An agent receives reward 2 immediately after its current action and reward 4 one step later, with no further rewards and discount factor gamma = 0.5. What is the return from the current time?

options.text: The return is 3, computed as 0.5 times 2 plus 0.5 times 4, because discounting starts on the immediate reward.
options.rationale: The immediate reward has temporal offset zero and therefore coefficient gamma to the zero power, which is one.

options.text: The return is 4, computed as 2 plus 0.5 times 4, because the next-step reward receives one factor of gamma.
options.rationale: Discounted return begins with the immediate reward and applies gamma once to a reward one step later.

options.text: The return is 6, computed as 2 plus 4, because gamma represents random termination rather than weighting delayed rewards in this trajectory.
options.rationale: Whatever probabilistic interpretation gamma may have, the return definition directly weights the delayed reward by gamma.

options.text: The current return stays the same after swapping rewards 2 and 4, because discounted value depends on reward amounts rather than temporal order.
options.rationale: Swapping the rewards gives 4 plus 0.5 times 2, which is 5 rather than the original return of 4.

questions.stem: A learner summarizes sequential decision making, exploration, and discounting. Which combined statement preserves the essential distinction in all three parts?

options.text: Actions change immediate reward but leave future data fixed; exploration and discounting then operate on an externally supplied trajectory distribution.
options.rationale: In sequential control, actions can change state transitions and therefore the future observations available to the learner.

options.text: A greedy policy gathers evidence about abandoned actions as time passes, while discounting handles delayed outcomes after that passive exploration.
options.rationale: An unchosen action supplies no new reward evidence, so a strictly greedy policy can remain locked into an early error.

options.text: Actions shape future experience, exploration buys information about uncertain choices, and discounting weights rewards according to their delay from the current decision.
options.rationale: The statement correctly connects policy-dependent data, the value of information, and the temporal indexing of return.

options.text: Actions shape future experience and exploration buys information, but gamma first discounts the reward received immediately after the current action.
options.rationale: The immediate reward has exponent zero in the standard return; gamma first appears on the next delayed reward.

questions.stem: From the current state, action A yields rewards 0 now and 4 one step later, while action B yields 2 now and 0 later. How does changing gamma from 0.5 to 0.25 affect their returns?

options.text: A and B remain tied under both values, because the order of a fixed pair of reward amounts does not affect discounted return.
options.rationale: Discounting attaches different weights to immediate and delayed rewards, so their temporal placement matters.

options.text: A changes from return 1 to return 0.5 while B changes from return 1 to return 0.5, because gamma discounts immediate rewards first.
options.rationale: The immediate reward receives coefficient one; gamma is applied to the reward one step later.

options.text: They tie at return 2 when gamma is 0.5; at gamma 0.25, A returns 1 while B returns 2, so B is preferred.
options.rationale: The respective returns are four gamma and two, so lowering gamma breaks the original tie in favor of immediate reward.

options.text: A receives the full delayed reward under both values because that reward belongs solely to the action immediately preceding its arrival.
options.rationale: Return from the current decision weights later rewards by their temporal distance rather than assigning them solely by recency.

questions.stem: A robot has an accurate predictor of immediate reward for state-action pairs seen in its log, but a proposed action can move it into states absent from that log. What prevents the reward predictor alone from establishing the action's long-run value?

options.text: The reward predictor converts the task into ordinary supervised learning, so its low logged error identifies the value of each proposed action sequence.
options.rationale: One-step reward labels do not by themselves specify how actions change later states or which later rewards follow.

options.text: Future states come from an external sampling process, so the proposed action affects immediate reward without affecting the later inputs presented to the robot.
options.rationale: The scenario explicitly allows the action to enter new states, making the future state distribution policy-dependent.

options.text: Accurate logged reward predictions identify the proposed policy's value despite missing transitions, since predictive accuracy removes the need for action support.
options.rationale: Logged one-step accuracy does not identify unobserved transition consequences or rewards in unsupported states.

options.text: Long-run value also depends on transition consequences, future policy choices, and adequate support or valid modeling for the states those choices reach.
options.rationale: A return couples immediate reward with the state trajectory generated by actions and the continuation policy.

questions.stem: An action yields reward 3 and transitions immediately to a terminal state. With discount factor gamma = 0.9, what target should a one-step value backup use for that action?

options.text: Use 3, because the immediate reward is undiscounted and the terminal state has no continuation value to add.
options.rationale: The Bellman target is reward plus gamma times continuation value, and the terminal continuation is zero.

options.text: Use 2.7, because gamma first multiplies the reward produced directly by the current action before any continuation is considered.
options.rationale: The current reward has delay zero and coefficient one; gamma multiplies the next-state continuation term.

options.text: Use the reward from the action before this one, because a terminal reward belongs to the latest prior action rather than the current backup.
options.rationale: The stated transition reward is attached to the current state-action transition and enters its backup directly.

options.text: Use 3 divided by 0.1, because gamma represents termination probability and a terminal observation expands into an infinite expected reward stream.
options.rationale: The observed transition already ends the episode, so there is no future stream to geometrically sum.

questions.stem: A news system replaces a broad exploration policy with one that shows mostly sports articles. A month later, its log contains mostly reactions to sports. Which conclusion respects how the policy generated this evidence?

options.text: The new reaction distribution is externally fixed, because content choices change immediate clicks without changing which feedback observations enter later logs.
options.rationale: Showing sports creates opportunities to observe sports reactions while withholding comparable feedback about other content.

options.text: The policy changed its own observation distribution; comparisons need logged propensities, overlap, experimentation, or defensible assumptions about unshown content.
options.rationale: Action selection controls which outcomes can be observed, so policy evaluation must address this endogenous missing data.

options.text: A reward predictor accurate on displayed sports articles identifies reactions to unshown topics, so policy support is unnecessary for evaluating broader recommendations.
options.rationale: In-support prediction quality does not validate counterfactual outcomes where the new log supplies little or no exposure.

options.text: Replace the policy with uniform random recommendations indefinitely, because equal exposure is the intrinsically optimal reward-information tradeoff for this system.
options.rationale: Random exposure can restore support, but uncertainty-aware or constrained exploration may obtain useful evidence at lower reward cost.

questions.stem: An agent receives +1 each time it moves closer to a goal and no corresponding penalty when it moves away. It learns to oscillate between two states rather than finish. What is the best diagnosis?

options.text: The locally positive progress reward changed return comparisons by making a repeatable cycle profitable, so policy preservation was not established.
options.rationale: Dense rewards alter the Bellman return unless their structure, such as valid potential shaping, preserves policy ordering.

options.text: Positive progress rewards preserve the goal policy because movements toward the goal remain locally desirable.
options.rationale: Local desirability does not prevent accumulated reward from favoring cycles or longer paths.

options.text: The shaping is safe if the terminal state's reward remains ranked above the reward of each intermediate state.
options.rationale: Discounted return depends on the full path, including repeatable intermediate rewards and duration.

options.text: The missing element is an undiscounted potential difference Phi(s') - Phi(s), independent of the MDP discount.
options.rationale: For a discounted MDP, the policy-invariant potential term uses gamma Phi(s') - Phi(s).

questions.stem: A discounted MDP has gamma = 0.9. A transition goes from a state with potential Phi(s) = 2 to one with Phi(s') = 5. Under potential-based shaping, what reward term is added for this transition?

options.text: +3.0, because the undiscounted increase in potential is the policy-invariant shaping term.
options.rationale: The next-state potential is discounted in a discounted MDP, giving 0.9 times 5 minus 2.

options.text: +2.5, because the term is gamma Phi(s') - Phi(s) = 0.9 times 5 minus 2.
options.rationale: This discounted potential difference telescopes across a trajectory in the policy-invariance result.

options.text: +5.0, because a positive destination potential can be used directly without changing the preferred policy.
options.rationale: Using destination potential alone can accumulate differently across paths and cycles.

options.text: +7.0, because preserving terminal-state ranking is enough even when intermediate potentials are summed.
options.rationale: Terminal ordering does not justify adding potentials; the specific discounted difference provides the guarantee.

questions.stem: An importance-sampling off-policy estimate uses 100,000 logged trajectories, but nearly all total weight is carried by 12 trajectories because target and behavior policies differ sharply. What is the central concern?

options.text: The logged returns transfer directly to the target policy because the raw trajectory count is large.
options.rationale: Policy mismatch changes which trajectories matter, and the effective weighted sample is much smaller than the row count.

options.text: Any zero-support target actions can be corrected by assigning them very large importance weights.
options.rationale: An action absent under the behavior policy has no observed outcome to reweight.

options.text: The estimate may have extreme variance and tiny effective sample size, so weight diagnostics and policy overlap are essential.
options.rationale: Concentration of weight means the nominal sample size badly overstates independent information about the target policy.

options.text: A learned dynamics model removes the overlap concern and turns unsupported target behavior into identified evidence.
options.rationale: Model extrapolation may trade variance for assumption-dependent bias; it does not create observed support.

questions.stem: A learned simulator predicts outcomes for actions rarely chosen by the logging policy. A target policy relies heavily on those actions, and no external validation covers that region. How should its model-based value estimate be described?

options.text: As the logged policy's observed return, because recorded rewards transfer directly to the target action sequence.
options.rationale: The target changes actions and state visitation, so its return is not the behavior policy's return.

options.text: As an unbiased importance-sampling estimate, because rare or absent target actions can be repaired by weighting.
options.rationale: Importance sampling needs behavior support for target actions and cannot validate model predictions where observations are absent.

options.text: As identified from data, because a fitted simulator removes the need for action coverage in the logged trajectories.
options.rationale: The simulator supplies extrapolating assumptions whose errors may compound in unsupported regions.

options.text: As assumption-sensitive extrapolation that needs overlap diagnostics, model checks, and preferably new coverage before strong claims.
options.rationale: A model can reduce variance and extend estimates, but unvalidated support gaps remain an identification risk.

questions.stem: Starting in A, an agent repeats the transition cycle A-to-B-to-A forever in a discounted MDP with gamma = 0.5, zero original rewards, Phi(A) = 2, and Phi(B) = 6. Under F(s,s') = gamma Phi(s') - Phi(s), what are the shaping return over the first two transitions and over the infinite trajectory?

options.text: The two-transition prefix is -1.5, and the endlessly repeated discounted cycles converge to -2 rather than diverging.
options.rationale: F(A,B) = 1 and F(B,A) = -5, so the first pair returns 1 + 0.5(-5) = -1.5. Repeated pairs are scaled by gamma^2 = 0.25, giving -1.5/(1 - 0.25) = -2.

options.text: The prefix is positive and the return diverges to positive infinity, because the positive A-to-B shaping term is collected again on each repeated cycle.
options.rationale: Repeating the positive edge also repeats the compensating B-to-A edge, and every later pair is geometrically discounted.

options.text: Using the plain potential differences gives shaping rewards +4 and -4, so they cancel even under the discounted return; both the two-edge prefix and infinite shaping return are zero.
options.rationale: Discounting prevents that claimed cancellation: the first pair is 4 + 0.5(-4) = 2, and repeated pairs yield 2/(1 - 0.25) = 8/3. The shaping term must use the return's gamma to telescope.

options.text: Both returns are zero because returning to A preserves the ordering of terminal potentials, so intermediate shaping terms need not be accumulated.
options.rationale: The trajectory is continuing rather than terminal, and its discounted intermediate terms yield the stated nonzero returns.

questions.stem: Training used planning discount 0.9 and shaping term 0.9 Phi(s') - Phi(s). A deployment planner changes its discount to 0.7 but keeps the old shaping term. Which conclusion follows?

options.text: Replace the term with Phi(s') - Phi(s), since an undiscounted potential difference works for either planner discount.
options.rationale: The telescoping policy-invariance result pairs the next-state potential with the active return discount.

options.text: The standard result no longer applies directly; use 0.7 Phi(s') - Phi(s) or prove the retained transformation separately.
options.rationale: Changing the planner's discount changes the potential difference required to telescope in that planner's return.

options.text: Keep the old term because rewards that usually move toward higher potential preserve the preferred policy.
options.rationale: Local progress does not substitute for the discounted potential form and can change path or cycle preferences.

options.text: Keep the old term if terminal-state ordering is unchanged, because intermediate discount mismatch leaves action rankings unaffected.
options.rationale: Different discounts and intermediate rewards can alter complete trajectory returns even with the same terminal ordering.

questions.stem: In a one-step logged decision, the behavior policy chose action a with b(a|x) = 0.2, the target policy has pi(a|x) = 0.8, and the observed reward is 3. Which off-policy account is correct before averaging across samples?

options.text: Use contribution 3 without a ratio, because an observed behavior-policy reward transfers directly to the target policy.
options.rationale: The target assigns different action probability, so the logged reward needs distribution-mismatch correction for this estimator.

options.text: Replace the contribution with a fitted reward prediction, because a learned model makes behavioral coverage irrelevant.
options.rationale: A model may provide an alternative estimate but does not change the observed sample's importance ratio or create missing support.

options.text: Use ratio 0.8 divided by 0.2 = 4 and weighted contribution 12; the denominator being positive is essential.
options.rationale: One-step importance sampling multiplies the observed reward by the target-to-behavior action-probability ratio.

options.text: The same calculation remains identified at b(a|x) = 0 by substituting a small denominator for the missing action.
options.rationale: A positive target probability over a zero behavior probability is a support failure, not a numerical smoothing problem.

questions.stem: For a one-step logged bandit sample, define the doubly robust estimate as sum_a pi(a)qhat(a) + pi(A)/b(A)[r - qhat(A)]. Here pi(A) = 0.75, pi(B) = 0.25, b(A) = 0.5, qhat(A) = 2, qhat(B) = 6, the logged action is A, and r = 4. Which calculation and interpretation are correct?

options.text: The estimate is 6: the target-model mean is 3 and the supported importance-weighted residual is 3; b(A) > 0 makes the logged correction well-defined.
options.rationale: The direct term is 0.75(2) + 0.25(6) = 3, while the correction is (0.75/0.5)(4 - 2) = 3.

options.text: The estimate is 4, because the observed reward can be carried directly from the behavior sample to the target policy without using either target probabilities or a correction.
options.rationale: A behavior-policy reward is not automatically a target-policy value; the stated estimator reweights its residual and adds a target-model baseline.

options.text: The estimate is 3, because fitting qhat removes the coverage requirement and makes the target-model mean sufficient, so the observed residual should be discarded.
options.rationale: The DR definition includes a supported residual correction; a learned model does not make that observed correction disappear.

options.text: The estimate is 6, and the identical calculation would remain identified if b(A) were zero by replacing the undefined ratio with an arbitrary small denominator.
options.rationale: The present ratio is defined because b(A) = 0.5. With zero behavior support there is no observed A sample from that region and no valid importance ratio to patch.
